newsitem.title: CHINA: FEATURE - Hong Kong return vindicates China clan.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Hong Kong return vindicates China clan.

text.p: Hong Kong's return to China after 156 years of British rule may be cause for celebration in Beijing, but for one man it is a vindication of an upright official who fell foul of his emperor.
The seizure of British opium by Qing court official Lin Zexu set the stage for Britain to send its gunboats and eventually claim Hong Kong island as its colonial prize.
"The return of Hong Kong is an important event for the Chinese people," said Ling Qing, a fifth-generation descendant of the Qing dynasty (1644-1911) official.
"It washes away the humiliation and rehabilitates China's prestige and dignity."
HEALING HISTORICAL WOUNDS
The return of the territory to Chinese rule at midnight on Monday, June 30, will also help to heal the historical wounds of a man who was arguably China's first anti-narcotics officer.
In 1838, the Daoguang emperor made Lin imperial commissioner to put a stop to the opium trade, deemed both morally offensive and a drain on China's precious reserves of silver.
Lin, one of the abler officials of the Qing court, blockaded the foreign settlement at Canton (Guangzhou) and ordered the opium to be turned over and destroyed.
The early results of his campaign were praised initially by his sponsors.

But he was removed and eventually banished to remote westernmost Xinjiang after a British armada blockaded the coastal ports of Xiamen and Ningbo and the mouth of the Yangtze river. By 1842 China gave up Hong Kong island under the Treaty of Nanjing.
"His treatment was unjust," said Ling. "It suited the political purpose of the emperor. In fact, he was a hero -- a man of integrity."
UNWISE TACTICS OR ANTI-DRUGS DRIVE?

Some historians dispute the wisdom of his tactics, saying he allowed British traders to dispose of much of the opium crop, with the British crown guaranteeing payment, at a time when there was a possibility of a huge glut of the drug.
His move also allowed opium to become an issue of free trade, as well as of Britain's ability to protect its subjects abroad.

Ling, a 74-year-old retired diplomat and former ambassador to the United Nations, said his ancestor should be viewed as a man who welcomed legitimate trade and wanted to absorb technology from the more advanced West.
"He did not ban normal trade," said Ling. "He asked the smugglers to sign a pledge not to continue the opium trade."
Ling now carries the historical torch for his ancestor as president of the Lin Zexu Foundation, which is dedicated to research on the 19th century official.
FROM COMMUNIST GUERRILLA TO U.N. ENVOY
Sitting in the library of his Beijing apartment, wearing spectacles and a grey business suit, he seems deceptively far removed from the young man who joined the communist underground in the 1940s.
It was then that he changed his name from Lin Moqing to protect his family from the ruling Nationalists who were hunting for communist agents.
He made his way to the hills of Yanan where Mao Zedong and his band of revolutionaries mapped their campaign to overthrow the Nationalist government, which eventually collapsed in 1949.
During his stint at the United Nations, he formally submitted to the world body the joint Sino-British declaration -- the 1984 agreement that returns Hong Kong to Chinese rule.

His bookshelves are adorned with reminders of that era -- photographs of former U.N. secretaries-general Kurt Waldheim and Javier Perez de Cuellar, as well as a snapshot of Ling dining over Peking duck with former U.S. Secretary of State Henry Kissinger.
Ling will probably be among the delegates at celebrations in Beijing marking the return of Hong Kong on July 1.
"I will celebrate the return along with the people of China," he says.
And, what if Commissioner Lin were around to see the recovery of its long-lost territory?
"He would be happy, of course."
